narrative: During the 1930s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in traditional practices and cultural identity. While specific information about this decade is limited, it is clear that protective hairstyles such as cornrows and box braids were already an integral part of African braiding practice and the African diaspora. These styles not only served a practical purpose by minimizing manipulation and exposure to environmental elements but also held significant cultural and symbolic value. The natural hair texture of Black and African women was also celebrated, with kinky hair being described as dense and distinct from other hair types. As the natural hair movement would later attest, embracing one's natural hair texture was (and continues to be) a powerful statement of identity and self-love. While there is no specific mention of hairstyles popular during this era, it is likely that traditional styles such as cornrows and braids were prevalent, given their enduring significance in African cultures.
